title: The algorithm will see you now
author: Deena Mousa

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Clinical teaming: AI accuracy may worsen joint decisions
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that standalone benchmark accuracy and human involvement do not guarantee better clinical decisions. It materially develops that position by identifying cross-hospital transfer failures, requiring local revalidation, documenting clinicians’ propagation of incorrect AI guidance, and treating autonomy as conditional on technical and regulatory safeguards.
qs: This means that individual hospitals or departments would need to retrain or revalidate today’s crop of tools before adopting them, even if they have been proven elsewhere.

Another [review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3240751/), this time from 2011, found that when a system gave incorrect guidance, clinicians were 26 percent more likely to make a wrong decision than unaided peers.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of jagged, task-specific capability, human-led augmentation and institution-dependent implementation, then materially extends it with radiology evidence. It shows how broader professional task mixes and elastic demand can turn productivity gains into work reallocation or expansion rather than occupational substitution, while cautioning that future capability gains could alter the pattern.
qs: Models can lift productivity, but their implementation depends on behavior, institutions and incentives.

st.t: Radiology assistance: Accuracy, teamwork and replacement diverge
st.an: Mousa directly supports the cluster’s distinction between benchmark capability and human replacement, while providing evidence that cross-hospital transfer, difficult cases and demographic underrepresentation require local validation or retraining before deployment.
qs: But replacing humans with AI is harder than it seems.
This means that individual hospitals or departments would need to retrain or revalidate today’s crop of tools before adopting them, even if they have been proven elsewhere.

kp.k: Benchmark success has not displaced radiologists
kp.d: Mousa contrasts radiology AI's benchmark achievements with continuing demand for human workers, rather than discussing legal services directly. She reports that CheXNet, released in 2017 and trained on more than 100,000 chest X-rays, outperformed a panel of board-certified radiologists at pneumonia detection. Despite Geoffrey Hinton's 2016 recommendation to stop training radiologists, the article reports 1,208 American diagnostic radiology residency positions in 2025, four percent more than 2024, all-time-high vacancy rates, and average 2025 income of $520,000, over 48 percent above 2015.
qs: CheXNet can detect pneumonia with greater accuracy than a panel of board-certified radiologists.
But demand for human labor is higher than ever.
The promise of AI in radiology is overstated by benchmarks alone.

kp.k: Narrow models automate only fragments of imaging work
kp.d: The article reports over 700 FDA-cleared radiology models, accounting for more than three-quarters of medical AI devices, but argues that product counts overstate task coverage. Most models address one finding in one image type; platforms aggregate separate answers rather than produce integrated image descriptions. Stroke, breast cancer and lung cancer account for about 60 percent of models but a minority of US imaging volume. Data availability and imaging complexity constrain coverage, with relatively few products for vascular, head and neck, spine and thyroid imaging.
qs: For every individual question, a new model is required.
The final output is a list of separate answers to specific questions, rather than a single description of an image.

Even with hundreds of imaging algorithms approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on the market, the combined footprint of today’s radiology AI models still cover only a small fraction of real-world imaging tasks.

kp.k: Performance deteriorates across hospitals and data conditions
kp.d: Among models in 2024 reporting their number of testing sites, 38 percent were tested using data from a single hospital. Mousa reports performance drops of as much as 20 percentage points on other hospitals' data and cites a pneumonia detection study illustrating this problem. She distinguishes avoidable overfitting from deeper differences in equipment and data generation, arguing that hospitals may need local retraining or revalidation even for tools proven elsewhere.
qs: Once deployed outside of the hospital where they were initially trained, models can struggle.
This means that individual hospitals or departments would need to retrain or revalidate today’s crop of tools before adopting them, even if they have been proven elsewhere.

kp.k: Training selection limits difficult-case and demographic performance
kp.d: The article argues that requirements for unambiguous diagnoses and clean images bias training datasets toward easier cases. A cited 2022 study found pneumonia detection faltered on subtle or mild disease and on conditions resembling pneumonia, including pleural effusions and atelectasis. An interviewed radiologist's report of surgical staples being labelled hemorrhages illustrates missing context, not a measured error rate. Mousa also reports underrepresentation of children, women and ethnic minorities, alongside missing demographic metadata that impedes bias correction.
qs: This skews performance towards the easiest cases, which doctors are already best at diagnosing, and away from real-world images.
Humans also benefit from context: one radiologist told me about a model they use that labels surgical staples as hemorrhages.
The result is that radiology models often predict only a narrow slice of the world.

kp.k: Historical computer aids disappointed despite approval and reimbursement
kp.d: Mousa uses mammography computer-aided diagnosis to distinguish controlled benchmark success from clinical outcomes. Following FDA approval in 1998 and Medicare reimbursement in 2001, a $7 additional payment helped accompany adoption in approximately 74 percent of US mammograms by 2010. Research covering 430,000 screening mammograms from 200,000 women at 43 community clinics between 1998 and 2002 found that the seven adopting clinics conducted 20 percent more biopsies without detecting more cancer. Across ten trials and seventeen studies of double reading, computer aids increased callbacks without raising detection, whereas two human readers detected more cancers with slightly fewer callbacks. Medicare ended additional reimbursement in 2018.
qs: Since the earliest days of computer-aided diagnosis, there has been a gulf between benchmark and clinical performance.
Computer-aided detection was worse than standard care, and much worse than another pair of eyes.

kp.k: Human deference can undermine assistive technology
kp.d: The author presents excessive deference to automated guidance as one explanation for the benchmark–clinical gap. A cited 2004 trial asked 20 breast screening specialists to read mammograms with computer prompts and a new group to read identical films without them: aided readers identified barely half the malignancies, versus 68 percent without assistance. The largest gap arose when software missed malignancy. A 2011 review found clinicians receiving incorrect system guidance were 26 percent more likely to make a wrong decision than unaided peers.
qs: In particular, doctors appear to defer excessively to assistive AI tools in clinical settings in a way that they do not in lab settings.
many doctors seemed to treat an absence of prompts as reassurance that a film was clean.

kp.k: Autonomous systems face higher regulatory safety requirements
kp.d: Mousa describes distinct FDA pathways for assistive or triage tools requiring physician interpretation and signature, and autonomous tools requiring stronger safeguards against unsuitable inputs. LumineticsCore illustrates narrowly bounded autonomy: adult patients without prior retinopathy, two macula-centred fundus photographs of at least 1,000 times 1,000 pixels, and mandatory abortion and referral for inadequate image quality. The article also states that retraining requires new approval, contributing to a lag between frontier capabilities and marketed systems; better evidence and performance could eventually overcome some barriers.
qs: Autonomous tools have to clear a much higher bar: they must demonstrate that the AI tool will refuse to read any scan that is blurry, uses an unusual scanner, or is outside its competence.
The bar is higher because, once the human disappears, a latent software defect could harm thousands before anyone notices.
This contributes to the market generally lagging behind frontier capabilities.

kp.d: The article reports diagnostic errors account for roughly a third of American malpractice payouts and attributes insurers' reluctance to cover autonomous systems to the potential for correlated harm across many patients. Physician-review requirements and AI exclusions impede hospitals' adoption. Digital Diagnostics offers an alternative allocation through product liability coverage and indemnity for LumineticsCore: reimbursement for damages traceable to algorithmic misclassification is conditional on exact compliance with the FDA label.
qs: Insurers believe that software makes catastrophic payments more likely than a human clinician, as a broken algorithm can harm many patients at once.
Without malpractice coverage, hospitals cannot afford to let algorithms sign reports.

kp.k: Adoption and reported implementation success remain limited
kp.d: Mousa argues that autonomous reads would need sufficient savings or throughput gains to justify hospitals seeking exceptions to credentialing and billing norms. A 2024 investigation estimated that 48 percent of radiologists used AI at all. A 2025 survey reported high success among only 19% of respondents who had begun piloting or deploying radiology AI use cases. These figures describe use and reported success, not measured autonomous replacement.
qs: For now, usage is too sparse to make a difference.

A [2025 survey](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12202002/#:~:text=Similarly%2C%20while%20most%20organizations%20have%20deployed%20AI%20in%20imaging%20and%20radiology%2C%20only%2019%25%20of%20them%20report%20a%20high%20degree%20of%20success%20in%20this%20area.) reported that only 19% of respondents who have started piloting or deploying AI use cases in radiology reported a “high” degree of success.

kp.k: Automating interpretation does not automate the entire occupation
kp.d: A study following staff radiologists at three hospitals in 2012 found direct image interpretation occupied only 36 percent of their time. Other responsibilities included overseeing examinations, communicating results, teaching residents and technologists, reviewing orders and changing protocols. Mousa therefore predicts that better interpretation systems may shift radiologists toward remaining tasks rather than eliminate their jobs; this is a conditional substitution argument, not an observed AI-driven time reallocation.
qs: Radiologists are useful for more than reading scans;
This means that, if AI were to get better at interpreting scans, radiologists may simply shift their time toward other tasks.
This would reduce the substitution effect of AI.

kp.k: Productivity gains can stimulate greater demand
kp.d: Mousa invokes Jevons paradox as a conditional mechanism and digitization as historical precedent. A Vancouver General study reported productivity increases of 27 percent for plain radiography and 98 percent for CT within a year of going filmless; the article states no radiologists were laid off. US imaging utilization per 1,000 insured patients increased 60 percent from 2000 to 2008, with more imaging per visit rather than a commensurate increase in visits. Reported median X-ray turnaround times fell from 76 to 38 hours for discharged emergency patients and from 84 to 35 hours for admitted patients. Faster turnaround enabled uses such as more routine whole-body trauma CT scans.
qs: As tasks get faster or cheaper to perform, we may also do more of them.
Yet, no radiologists were laid off.
In this case, when these scans got cheaper in terms of waiting time, demand for those scans increased.

kp.k: Early diffusion depends on institutions, incentives and task diversity
kp.d: The author argues that radiology's first decade of AI diffusion favours human–machine combinations because task coverage, patient counselling, malpractice and accreditation remain obstacles. Multitask foundation models and different training sets may improve coverage, and sharp capability increases could change the balance. She explicitly limits generalization by contrasting platform moderation, reporting machines make 94 percent of Facebook and 98 percent of Instagram moderation decisions. For jobs with diverse tasks, high stakes and elastic demand, she predicts software initially creates more human work, not less.
qs: Each hurdle makes full substitution the expensive, risky option and human plus machine the default.
Sharp increases in AI capabilities could certainly alter this dynamic, but it is a useful model for the first years of AI models that benchmark well at tasks associated with a particular career.
In many jobs, tasks are diverse, stakes are high, and demand is elastic. When this is the case, we should expect software to initially lead to more human work, not less.
Models can lift productivity, but their implementation depends on behavior, institutions and incentives.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mousa argues that radiology AI's benchmark successes have not translated into wholesale replacement of radiologists; initially, augmentation and potentially greater demand for human work are more likely.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about radiology, not a direct claim about legal services. Mousa identifies three limits on substitution: narrow task coverage and weaker performance outside test settings; regulatory and insurance barriers to autonomous diagnosis; and the substantial share of radiologists' work that is not image interpretation. She further argues that human reliance on assistive tools can itself impair clinical performance. She predicts that improved AI could shift radiologists toward other duties and, by reducing costs or waiting times, stimulate additional imaging demand. Her broader inference concerns knowledge jobs with diverse tasks, high stakes and elastic demand, rather than all occupations. Hinton's prediction about ending radiologist training is presented as a contrast, not as Mousa's own forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Mousa supports her argument with benchmark results, workforce and adoption statistics, clinical studies, regulatory examples, an interview anecdote and historical evidence about imaging productivity and demand.
pts.d: For technical capability, Mousa cites CheXNet's pneumonia benchmark performance and over 700 FDA-cleared radiology models. For continued human demand, she reports 1,208 diagnostic radiology residency positions in 2025, a 4 percent increase over 2024, and average radiologist income of $520,000, over 48 percent above 2015. For limited generalisation, she reports that 38 percent of models disclosing testing-site counts in 2024 were tested at one hospital and that performance can fall by as much as 20 percentage points out of sample. She cites research on demographic gaps and difficult images, alongside an unnamed radiologist's anecdote about surgical staples being labelled hemorrhages. Historical mammography evidence includes 430,000 screenings of 200,000 women at 43 clinics: adopting computer-aided detection was associated with 20 percent more biopsies without additional cancer detection. A 2011 review found clinicians receiving incorrect system guidance were 26 percent more likely to make a wrong decision than unaided peers. Regulatory and insurance evidence includes LumineticsCore's restricted autonomous clearance and vendor indemnity. Adoption evidence comprises a 2024 estimate that 48 percent of radiologists use AI and a 2025 survey in which only 19 percent of respondents piloting or deploying radiology AI reported high success. A 2012 study at three hospitals attributed only 36 percent of radiologists' time to direct image interpretation. As historical support for demand expansion, Mousa cites digitisation at Vancouver General increasing productivity by 27 percent for plain radiography and 98 percent for CT within a year, alongside a 60 percent rise in US imaging utilisation per 1,000 insured patients from 2000 to 2008. These digitisation findings are an analogy supporting her AI prediction, not measurements of AI's employment effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The argument concerns the first decade of radiology AI diffusion through 2025 and makes a conditional, near-term prediction rather than ruling out eventual substitution.
pts.d: Mousa contrasts predictions made in 2016 and CheXNet's release in 2017 with workforce and adoption evidence through 2025. Continued reliance on humans is conditional on limited model coverage, unreliable transfer across hospitals, behavioural responses to assistance, regulatory requirements and malpractice coverage. Hospitals may need local retraining or revalidation, while retraining can trigger renewed regulatory approval. Autonomous deployment requires both suitable technical performance and sufficient savings or throughput gains to justify changes to credentialing and billing practices. Foundation models and improved training data may reduce technical constraints, and sharp capability gains could change the balance. The prediction of increased human work is specifically qualified by task diversity, high stakes and elastic demand; Mousa contrasts radiology with more extensively automated platform content moderation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups include radiologists, hospitals, patients, referring clinicians, AI vendors, regulators and insurers, with effects varying by imaging task and patient population.
pts.d: Radiologists may gain productivity and move toward supervision, consultation, teaching and protocol decisions rather than lose their jobs. Hospitals face integration, local validation, approval and liability barriers to autonomous use. Referring clinicians may order more imaging when turnaround times fall. Patients may benefit from quicker diagnosis but also face false positives, additional procedures, missed disease and automation-related clinical errors. Mousa reports poorer model performance for underrepresented children, women and ethnic minorities, and limited product coverage outside common imaging use cases. Vendors must meet regulatory requirements and may need to assume liability to enable autonomous deployment; insurers are concerned about correlated harm from software defects. These are claims about healthcare participants, not findings about lawyers or legal-service buyers.
